On the evidence, both the plaintiff and the defendant were in the course of employment for Schedule 1 employers at the time of the accident.  There is an onus on a party alleging a distinct departure from employment to bring evidence to support the allegation.  There was no such evidence in this case.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for an onset of back pain in May 1985, which the worker claimed was related to a compensable accident in May 1984.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue entitlement for a number of other disabilities at the Board.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Future economic loss {FEL} (time periods) (extension); Intervening causes (undermotivation); Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation); Temporary partial disability (duration of benefits)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back strain in June 1980 when she bent down.  She returned to work in September 1990 but had a recurrence in January 1991.  She returned for a work trial in March 1992 but stopped working again in April 1992.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting only 50% benefits for temporary partial disability from June 19, 1992, to July 1, 1992.  The Hearings Officer did not consider entitlement to temporary benefits after July 1, as the worker then started receiving FEL benefits.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer which granted the worker entitlement to a provisional psychiatric award beyond its expiration date.  The worker claimed that the Hearings Officer should have made the award permanent, rather than provisional.

The worker was receiving a 20% pension and a full supplement under s. 147(2) of the Act.  The worker sought a full commutation of her pension to pay down her mortgage as she was afraid of losing her home.

The worker was injured when a chair on which she was sitting collapsed.  The Board originally transferred 50% of the costs of the claim to the manufacturer of the chair and 50% to the supplier.  However, the Hearings Officer reversed this decision, and all the costs were transferred back to the employer.  The employer appealed.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (error of law)
DecSummary: The employer applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board confirming a penalty assessment for the years 1975-77.  Previously, a penalty for the years 1973-75 had been cancelled by the Board.
The worker slipped and fell, striking his head.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement for psychological disability.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further entitlement at the Board.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (escalation); Earnings basis (maximum); Earnings basis (recurrences) (prior pension award)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable accident in 1979.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding the earnings basis for calculation of benefits for a recurrence in 1987.

He also received an additional 7.5% pension as a multiple factor.  He laid off work again in November 1989 and received full benefits until January 1990.  In July 1991, his pension was increased, retroactive to April 1990, to 19% for the right knee, 18% for the left knee and a 9% multiple factor.

The Hearings Officer decision was based on a diagnosis of piriformis syndrome, which could not be related to the compensable accidents.  However, that diagnosis was subsequently abandoned.  The current diagnosis was compatible with recurrent back problems related to the compensable accidents.

The worker was awarded a s. 147(4) supplement from the time the 15% pension was awarded in July 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement to a supplement from July 1989 for the first accident.
The worker was suffering from right carpal tunnel syndrome.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits from July to September 1991.

The worker was appealing denial of a pension for organic or psychotraumatic disability.  The worker wanted the Panel to consider entitlement for chronic pain.  The Panel found that it had jurisdiction since the Hearings Officer effectively ruled on entitlement for a psychotraumatic and behavioural disorder.
The worker suffered a back injury in May 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement after March 1990.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further entitlement at the Board.  [3 pages]

[3 pages]

Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, including a number of reports that had been edited by the Board.  The issue in dispute was entitlement to an older worker supplement.  Eligibility to an older worker supplement is based on a worker being a poor candidate for rehabilitation due to both compensable and non-compensable barriers.  Accordingly, the worker's medical history, dealing with non-compensable conditions, was directly relevant to the issue in dispute and was released to the employer.  [4 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 981/94 was denied.  New medical evidence did not address the finding that the compensable accident was not a significant contributing factor to the ongoing organic or chronic pain symptoms experienced by the worker.  [4 pages]

Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for a personal reference which was not relevant.  The fact that the worker was no longer employed by the employer did not prevent the employer from obtaining access.  Any non-cooperation by the employer in the course of the claim, as alleged by the worker, could not be dealt with in this forum.  [4 pages]

A truck driver appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a knee disability.  The Panel found that the worker had a cystic meniscus which may have predisposed the knee to injury but that the nature of the worker's job, requiring use of his knee in loading the truck, was a significant contributing factor to a torn meniscus and development of osteoarthritis.

DecKeywords: Environmental hypersensitivity; Exposure (phenol); Health care (medical aid) (alternative treatment); Health care (necessary)
DecSummary: The worker claimed that she suffered a disability in 1966 as a result of the exposure to phenol, which was used to clean the laboratory where she worked.  In 1993, the Appeal Board found that the worker was hypersensitive to phenol, in addition to other chemicals and substances to which she had been hypersensitive prior to the accident.  Giving the worker every benefit of the doubt, the Appeal Board granted temporary benefits for the period of acute symptoms from December 1966 to February 1967, and a 15% pension.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Adjournment (witness availability); Three week rule (documents); Transcript

Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

The worker's hours were gradually increased to seven, but she had to lay off work in July 1992 and had not returned to work since.

The worker appealed a decision denying him supplementary benefits.  The Board denied such benefits because it found that the worker initially lost his job for reasons unrelated to his disability and subsequently he was medically capable of performing his preaccident job with his 10% organic disability.  However, the worker was also claiming benefits for a chronic pain disability and that claim had not as yet been finally determined by the Board.  The extent of the worker's disability was in issue in the present appeal.  Acceptance of the worker's claim for chronic pain would be a factor in determining this issue.

The worker was involved in a compensable motor vehicle accident in 1987.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement for organic back disability and denying entitlement for non-organic disability.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (employer assessment) (amalgamation of accounts); Experience rating (NEER) (amalgamation of accounts); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board)
DecSummary: The employer was a large corporation with headquarters outside Ontario. The Board amalgamated the accounts, effective January 1993, and closed the accounts being amalgamated, thus eliminating these firms' NEER retrospective rating for two years.  The employer appealed.

DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable injury in July 1990.  In January 1992, she attended a meeting with her rehabilitation counsellor and her employer. The worker's doctor was on holiday.  He signed the plan when he returned on February 7, 1992.  The worker took the approved plan to the counsellor on February 10, but was told that she had been expected at work on January 27, and that her entitlement to rehabilitation services and supplementary benefits was being terminated.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the termination.

The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that a die-dipper job offered to the worker was not suitable and that, accordingly, the worker was entitled to vocational rehabilitation services.

The worker suffered a back injury in 1973.  Entitlement was eventually extended to cover a right knee injury.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement for right knee disability beginning in 1989.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a low back injury.

DecKeywords: Evidence (weight); Investigation by Tribunal (post-hearing) (clarification of medical report)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for an unwitnessed accident.  Early reports of the accident referred to a recurrence of a prior problem and did not describe a lifting accident as now claimed by the worker.

The worker was appealing a decision of the Hearings Officer denying vocational rehabilitation services and a s. 147(2) supplement subsequent to March 1993.

The worker suffered a knee injury for which he was awarded a 3% pension, later increased to 5% and then to 7%.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the 7% pension.

The worker suffered a low back injury in 1979 for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a s. 147(4) supplement.

DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying entitlement for a back condition.  The worker submitted that the Appeal Board relied on a misdiagnosis. The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officers denying the employer's request to designate its three vice-presidents as executive officers.
The worker injured his back in 1981 and was awarded a 15% pension in 1983 which was increased to 20% in March 1992.

DecSummary: The worker was diagnosed as having bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in October 1990.  In November 1990 she began part-time employment with another company.  In late 1992, the worker obtained a second part-time job.  She averaged 65 hours monthly in the first job and 85 hours monthly for both jobs, in 1993. The worker decided not to pursue a s. 54 ruling from the Board.

In this case, the worker was entitled to his pension as of 1982.

One year later she attempted an eight week work trial with the accident employer that was to involve progressively longer shifts.  The Board terminated the worker's benefits one month after the end of the work trial, on the basis that she claimed to be totally disabled.  The Board subsequently denied the worker a FEL award on the basis that she had declined employment which the Board deemed to be suitable.  The Board advised the worker that she had reached maximum medical rehabilitation and that her injury was now being considered as a chronic pain disability claim. DecKeywords: Executive officers; In the course of employment (dual purpose test); Right to sue
DecSummary: The plaintiff claimed that he was an executive officer of the car dealership, even though he was not listed as such in corporate documents.  A director of a corporation is understood to be its directing mind.  An executive officer can be something less than that but must have a reasonable degree of responsibility, not only for a specific portion of the corporation but for the entity as a whole.  An executive officer must have some working knowledge of the financial status of the corporation and must share in some of the responsibility for the overall direction and health of the corporation.

The Board had dismissed the worker's claim for benefits for silicosis as X-rays taken during his lifetime failed to disclose any evidence of silicosis.  The worker's widow appealed that decision, as well as a decision denying her dependency benefits on the basis that the worker's lung cancer was not caused by his employment as a gold miner.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a left inguinal hernia, which the worker claimed was caused by a lifting incident at work.

The Board apparently based its decision on the 1991 pension assessment indicating a possibility of deterioration of the worker's condition.  However, functional abilities evaluations in 1992 and 1993 indicated no deterioration and, if any change, some improvement in his condition.  The worker has not required treatment from his treating specialist since 1991 and has been able to work since returning to work in April 1993.

The worker sought medical attention for back complaints in February 1986.  In July 1986 she underwent back surgery.  She left her job as a factory worker in October 1986 because she was incapable of performing work that involved repetitive bending.  She updated her office skills and began working as a secretary in December 1986.

DecSummary: The claimant was a seasonal worker who was off work for the winter.  A owned an island which he wanted to develop for cottages.  He bulldozed a hydro right of way through the island, cutting down a considerable number of trees to do so.  A and E entered into an arrangement whereby E would remove the trees from the island at no charge.  The claimant approached A and offered to help clear the trees.  A told the claimant to speak to E.  E agreed to pay the claimant a certain amount per cord to clear the trees.  The claimant was injured while doing this work.  The claimant appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer finding that the claimant was not a worker within the meaning of the Act.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further entitlement at the Board.  [3 pages]

A co-worker confirmed that the worker performed a job that day which was more strenuous than usual and that the worker subsequently was in pain.  Reports from the employer stated that the worker complained of back pain in November 1974.  The worker stopped working in January 1975 because he was unable to tolerate his back pain.  He did not report the accident to the Board until August 1977.  The worker had a pre-existing degenerative disc condition.

The person cleaning the cafeteria floor on which the worker slipped was a hospital employee.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting a 15% pension for chronic pain. The Panel concluded that the worker was entitled to a 30% pension.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a pension for permanent disability resulting from an accident in 1989.

The worker was not required to attend a medical examination requested by the employer.  The employer's request was made pursuant to a collective agreement.  The Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over this matter.  Further, the worker had not appealed the decision of the Claims Adjudicator.  Accordingly, there was no issue in dispute.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Continuity (of complaint)

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (disabled by non-compensable condition)

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying entitlement for a back condition which the worker claimed was related to compensable accidents in 1958, 1960 and 1965.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Availability for employment (disabled by non-compensable condition); Temporary partial disability (level of benefits)

The worker suffered bilateral elbow tendinitis in 1982.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement in 1989 for bilateral elbow and wrist disability.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a breathing disability and denying full benefits from October 1991 to May 1992.

The Board granted entitlement for psychotraumatic disability, diagnosed as post-traumatic stress disorder, related to the motor vehicle accident. One year after the surgery, he began to experience a burning and tingling sensation in his upper thigh, followed by numbness.  The worker continued working, but repetitive bending and reaching aggravated his thigh symptoms.  He had to stop working due to the discomfort in February 1993.  The worker suffered from meralgia paresthetica.  This condition involved entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.
The hearing was adjourned by the Panel as it needed additional evidence regarding numerous prior claims.  [5 pages]

On appeal, the worker was granted a 1% sustainability award.  In March 1992, the worker was laid off.  The Board refused to reopen the worker's VR file.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding the earnings basis for calculation of benefits and confirming the 1% sustainability award.
The worker suffered severe lacerations of his left arm in a chain saw accident. The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting a 2% pension for permanent disability.

The worker's supplement under s. 147(2) was cancelled after the worker was unable to complete four different work trials.  On appeal, the Hearings Officer granted a s. 147(4) supplement from February 1993 to the date of the hearing in January 1994, and a s. 147(2) supplement thereafter.  The worker appealed denial of a s. 147(2) supplement from  February 1993 to January 1994.
A 56-year-old worker suffered a back injury in a fall in September 1987.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying s. 147(2) supplementary benefits after February 1992.

The representative later argued that it was the termination itself that caused the worker's psychological problems.

He was entitled to temporary total benefits until December 1992, then to a FEL award with a supplement under s. 43(9).  The Board, by granting temporary benefits until December 1992 but no FEL award, had not implemented the Panel's decision correctly.  [4 pages]

The Board denied a FEL award on the grounds that the worker had refused suitable work at no wage loss.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer confirming the denial of a FEL award.

The worker withdrew her appeal of a decision denying s. 147(4) benefits.  [3 pages]

This provides a three year window for adjustments to the initial claim.  The cut-off for the third year of the 1989 NEER assessment was September 30, 1992.  In this case, the employer was granted 75% SIEF relief regarding a 1989 claim by the Tribunal on December 22, 1992.  The Board refused to readjust the 1989 NEER assessment since the SIEF relief was granted outside the three year window.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement for low back disability.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hepatitis C and cirrhosis.  The worker worked as a cleaner in a hospital laboratory from 1978 to 1985.  During this time, she had numerous cuts and needle stick injuries.

In March 1958, the worker underwent surgery for a herniated lumbosacral disc with nerve root pressure on the right side of the first sacral root.
