DecKeywords: Penalties; Board Directives and Guidelines (penalty assessments) (policy change); Merits and justice; Retroactivity (policy change)
DecSummary: The employer entered the NEER program in January 1986.  In May 1988, it was assessed a penalty under s. 103(8) for the years 1984-1986, notwithstanding that it was enrolled in the NEER program in 1986.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the penalty assessment.

The worker developed carpal tunnel syndrome in 1986, for which she was awarded a 7.5% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement to a s. 147(4) supplement from August 1991 to March 1993.
The worker appealed her 25% pension rating for a chronic pain disability relating to her right knee.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Causation (medical evidence) (standard of proof); Exposure (chemicals) (foam); Headaches; Medical opinion (headaches) (migraine)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for a condition described as migraine headaches.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for an accident which the worker claimed he suffered a work in May 1991.  The employer claimed that the worker quit his job in a dispute about a pay raise.

DecKeywords: Significant contribution (of compensable accident to disability)
DecSummary: The worker fell off a chair in 1981.  The worker's estate appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement to temporary benefits for chest surgery in 1990 and denying a pension.

DecKeywords: Pensions (assessment) (shoulder); Pensions (Rating Schedule) (chronic pain); Temporary partial disability
DecSummary: The worker experienced shoulder pain in August 1985.  She received temporary benefits until February 1986 when she returned to her regular work.  The worker stopped working in May 1988 due to shoulder pain.  In Decision No. 180/94I the panel found that the worker had some degree of work-related permanent disability, but referred the matter back to the Board to determine the level of the worker's permanent disability and any periods of total disability.

The worker suffered a low back injury in 1981, for which he was awarded a 20% pension for organic disability and a 20% pension for psychiatric disability.  The worker had a recurrence in July 1988 and received temporary benefits until January 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits after January 1990.

The worker was appealing a decision of the Reinstatement Officer denying vocational rehabilitation services after November 1993.  The hearing was adjourned so it could be heard together with the appeal by the worker of a decision of a Hearings Officer regarding temporary benefits in 1993.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Chronic pain; Delay (onset of symptoms); Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a left leg injury in November 1985 when he was struck from behind by a tow motor.  He returned to work in March 1986 but stopped working again in September 1986.  He made a further unsuccessful attempt to return to work in February 1987.  The worker appealed denial of benefits for a number of conditions and denial of further temporary benefits.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement after July 1987 for neck and low back disability.

DecKeywords: Medical report (opinion of treating doctor preferred); Temporary total disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a rotator cuff tear in January 1990.  The Board granted temporary total disability benefits until the worker returned to modified work in July 1990, but later reversed that decision and found that the worker was fit to return to modified work in May 1990.  The worker appealed.
The worker suffered a back and neck injury in June 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain.

The worker was diagnosed with dermatitis in 1978 but did not lose any time from work until July 1984.  In 1992, she was awarded a 5% pension retroactive to July 1984.  In 1993, the pension was increased to 15% retroactive to September 1983, which was three months before the worker's doctor wrote to the Board stating that the dermatitis had flared up.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying retroactivity of the pension to 1978.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (distinct departure test); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Right to sue
DecSummary: The issue in this s. 17 application was whether A and L were in the course of their employment at the time of an automobile accident.  L was A's supervisor but they were also long-time friends.  L was driving the employer's van at the time of the accident.  They had an appointment to do a job at a client's premises.  There was some talk of delaying or even postponing that job, as L wanted to show A a house he had recently sold.  L and A often began their day with breakfast at a doughnut shop.  L stated he would not have finalized his plans for the day until they had had breakfast at the doughnut shop.
The hearing was adjourned, so that information could be obtained regarding a fraud investigation being conducted by the Board.  [3 pages]

The worker claimed that he got into a verbal argument with his foreman, and that the worker fell, injuring his back and shoulder, when the foreman frightened the worker by striking the worker's time card.

A cashier suffered left neck, back and hip injury from the nature of her work.  She received temporary total disability benefits for two weeks in July 1987, and 50% temporary partial disability benefits from July 1987 to March 1993, when she was awarded a 15% pension for chronic pain.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the reduction to 50% temporary benefits and confirming the 15% pension.

The worker worked as a sewing machine operator from 1971 to July 1986, when she stopped working due to low back disability with pain radiating down her right leg.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement.

The worker suffered from a condition diagnosed as leukocytoclastic vasculitis.  The Board granted benefits for certain periods in 1989 for aggravation of a preexisting non-compensable condition.  However, the Board denied further benefits from November 1989 to September 1990.  The worker appealed denial of further benefits.

DecKeywords: Independent operator (courier); Right to sue; Worker (test) (control test)
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The issue was whether the plaintiff, a courier, was a worker or an independent operator.
The worker was not entitled to benefits for right hip osteoarthritis, as the Panel found that it was not related to his 1962 work accident.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Procedure (absent parties) (access to worker file); Procedure (conference call)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision to release information in the worker's file to the employer.  The Tribunal corresponded with the parties to notify them of the time when the hearing would be held by conference call.  The worker was not available at the scheduled time.  As the worker  had not contacted the Tribunal to advise of any difficulties, the Panel decided to hear the employer's submissions.  The Panel had already received written submissions from both parties.  The Tribunal Counsel Office attempted to contact the worker for a further five days after the hearing, but was unsuccessful.  As every reasonable effort had been extended to ensure that the worker was allowed to participate, a decision should now be reached.

The worker suffered compensable fractures and soft tissue injury to his lower leg, ankle and foot in March 1982.  In August 1982, while undertaking therapy at DRC, the worker's crutches slipped on a wet floor and he fell on his buttocks.  The worker appealed a decision denying him benefits for ongoing low back difficulties arising from the fall at DRC.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for fibrositis which the worker claimed was related to compensable accidents in 1957 and 1984, or to the nature of her work in a poultry processing plant.

DecKeywords: Apportionment (pensions) (co-existing conditions); Pensions (AMA Guides) (nervous system disorders)
DecSummary: The Board granted the worker a 5% pension for organic brain dysfunction.  In Decision No. 681/94I, the Panel directed the Board to review the pension rating.
The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The issue was whether the plaintiff was a worker or an executive officer.
The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the worker's death from lung cancer.

DecKeywords: Chronic obstructive lung disease; Heart condition; Silicosis; Mining (gold)
DecSummary: The worker was a gold miner from 1937 to 1970.  The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying dependency benefits for the worker's death.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Continuity (of treatment)
DecSummary: The worker suffered right rotator cuff tendonitis in 1972 as a result of repetitive overhead work.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits in 1990.

The worker suffered a compensable injury for which he was awarded a 15% pension.  The pension was commuted on the application of the worker.  The pension was later increased by an additional 5%.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying commutation of the additional 5% pension.

The worker suffered a back injury in October 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting only 50% benefits for temporary disability from November 1992 to December 1992 and terminating benefits in December 1992.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back disability in 1990.  Considering lack of continuity of treatment and ability to do heavy work, the Panel found that the worker's condition was not related to a compensable low back injury suffered in 1984.  However, the Panel found that the condition was related to the worker's work in 1990.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (appealable issue); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board) (refusal to refer to Hearings Officer); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (interlocutory appeal); Natural justice (removal of representative); Parties (representation) (removal of representative)
DecSummary: The worker was appealing a decision of the Decision Review Specialist denying continuing entitlement.  The worker wanted to appeal this decision directly to the Tribunal since the Board would not schedule a Hearings Officer hearing if the worker continues to be represented by his current representative.

A 38-year-old truck driver suffered a heel injury in 1991.  He was unable to return to work as a truck driver.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer denying sponsorship for training as a commercial pilot and flight instructor.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (disabled by non-compensable condition)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable low back injury in April 1990.  In June 1990, he was involved in a non-compensable motor vehicle accident.  In October 1990, his benefits were reduced to 50%.  In March 1991, benefits were terminated.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the termination of temporary benefits.

The worker suffered a fractured leg in an accident in August 1985.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from May 1988 to October 1988, and from November 1988 to July 1990.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying partial commutation of the worker's 15% pension for the purpose of business investment.  The worker's business plan was incomplete, inconsistent and incoherent.  He had no understanding of business relationships generally or of the particular arrangements in this case.  He did not appear to have the capacity necessary to manage a business enterprise and it was also questionable if he was medically capable of performing the duties required.

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, vocational (program not offered by Board)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in March 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting only 50% benefits for temporary partial disability from March 1987 to July 1988.

The worker  appealed a Hearings Officer decision confirming the level (10%) of his provisional pension.  Since the date of the Hearings Officer decision, the pension had been made permanent, but still at the 10% level.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Availability for employment (refusing suitable work)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision which closed his vocational rehabilitation file, reduced his temporary benefits and denied him a FEL supplement on the basis that he refused suitable work.  The worker was a mushroom picker when a four pound object fell a distance of three feet and struck his neck and shoulder.  The worker returned to modified work with the accident employer, but left after less than two hours.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying commutation of his 10% pension, valued at about $41,000, which he wanted to pay property tax arrears and to reduce his mortgage.

The worker was appealing denial of a pension relating to an accident in 1977.  The worker was receiving a pension for an accident in 1984.  The appeal was withdrawn after discussion of the downside risk regarding the earnings basis for calculation of benefits if the calculation was based on 1977 earnings.  [3 pages]
The worker suffered a neck injury in June 1990.  The worker and employer appealed decisions regarding entitlement to vocational rehabilitation in 1991 and 1992.

On the day before the scheduled hearing, the employer's representative requested an adjournment of the employer's appeal pending resolution of other matters still at the Board.  The Tribunal's Appeals Administrator told the representative that, in the circumstances, the adjournment would be granted if he obtained the consent of the worker.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the worker's entitlement to benefits for low back disability.  The worker returned to work on June 5, 1991, after a company lay-off of five months.  On June 8, he worked overtime loading about 300 boxes, each weighing 40 to 60 pounds.  On June 9, he played baseball.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for traumatic hearing loss in the left ear.  The worker suffered back and shoulder injuries in 1965 when he was struck by a steel beam swinging from a crane.  The worker did not claim entitlement for hearing loss until 1973.

DecKeywords: Impairment of earning capacity; Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: The worker suffered compensable rotator cuff tendonitis, for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement to a temporary supplement under s. 45(5) of the pre-1989 Act from March 1988 to May 1988.

The worker sustained a compensable back strain in November 1976 when he fell and his toolbox landed on top of him.  He returned to construction work in May 1977.  A June 1977 medical report stated that the worker had no pain or restriction of movement.  In 1980, he had a flare-up of back pain brought on by shovelling snow.  No degenerative changes had been noted in x-rays of the worker's spine taken earlier in 1980.  In 1984 he fell from a ladder and hurt his lower back.  In 1991 the worker experienced low back pain resulting from starting a snowmobile. A CT scan in 1992 showed degenerative change and a bulging disc in the worker's low back.

The worker was receiving a 40% pension for injuries to his lung, kidney, lumbar back and thoracic back which were sustained in a 1983 motor vehicle accident.  In March 1988, while descending an icy stairway, he fell and broke his left ankle.  The worker claimed that his disability caused him to favour his right leg and that the extra pressure on the left ankle resulted in his fall.  The worker had been experiencing pain in his right knee and foot, which was not related to his compensable condition, for some time prior to the accident.  He had gout in his right foot.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (natural justice) (written reasons)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal a decision of the WCB Appeal Board confirming his pension for a psychiatric disability at the 18% level.  The Appeal Board concluded that there was a minimal relationship between the worker's neurosis and the work accident so that the worker was entitled only to 30% of his assessed disability for the neurosis.  The Appeal Board found that the worker had an assessed disability of 60% due to the neurosis.

The worker suffered a left shoulder and back strain in July 1990 while moving a heavy object.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits and vocational rehabilitation after July 1991.

The worker was appealing a decision denying the costs of a motor scooter and van lift.  The worker was suffering from a number of conditions for which there had not been a final decision from the Board.  At a pre-hearing conference arranged by the Tribunal Counsel Office, the hearing was adjourned to allow the worker to obtain a representative.  If the worker does not notify the Tribunal by a specified date, the appeal will be considered withdrawn.  [4 pages]

The worker suffered a head and neck injury in 1975, for which he was awarded a 5% pension.  He continued to suffer from chronic muscle contraction headaches.  The Board paid for chiropractic treatment for a few months in 1991 and 1992.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying payment for chiropractic treatment after May 1992.

The worker appealed a decision denying entitlement to temporary supplementary benefits, from November 1991 to July 1993, because he was not cooperating with his vocational rehabilitation caseworker.  In February 1990, while the worker was employed as a groundsman, his glove became caught in a wood chipping machine.  Three fingers were amputated as a result of that accident.

The worker appealed a decision denying him ongoing temporary benefits after December 1989.  The Hearings Officer found that the worker was fully recovered from his organic low back condition which was caused by a fall in April 1989.  The worker wanted the Panel to deal with his claim for chronic pain, although the issue was currently still before the Decision Review Branch at the Board.  The employer stated that it was not prepared to deal with this issue.
The worker withdrew her appeal after it was explained that there was a downside risk in appealing the level of her pension.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (commutation) (rehabilitative measure); Commutation (business investment)
DecSummary: The worker was entitled to a partial commutation of his low back pension to purchase a used truck with an air ride frame, cab and seat.  This would enable him to become an independent owner/operator.
The worker suffered compensable back injuries in 1968, 1985 and 1987.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement.
The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement to the worker for a left inguinal hernia.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary) (participation in rehabilitation)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in 1979 for which he was awarded a 20% pension.  The Hearings Officer granted further VR services and a s. 147(2) supplement effective the day of the Hearings Officer hearing in May 1993.  The worker appealed denial of a supplement from January 1992 to May 1993.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment (opinion of the Board); Supplements, transitional provisions (rehabilitation) (cooperation)
DecSummary: The worker suffered compensable low back injuries in 1981, 1984 and 1987.  He was awarded a 15% pension in April 1989 for chronic pain disorder.  In May 1989, the worker obtained part-time work as a car salesman on commission.  He did not earn much money at this job, but he could adjust his hours so as to best manage with his back pain.  In July 1989, the accident employer advised the Board that it had a light job for the worker, for which it would provide a modified workstation.  The worker testified that he went to the accident employer to inquire about the modified work, but was told that his old job was waiting for him.  The worker stayed on at the car sales job, but stopped working in November 1989 due to increased back pain.
The worker suffered a shoulder injury in September 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying supplementary benefits after September 1992.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (excavation); Class of employer (trucking); Legal precedent (consistency)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer finding that the employer was properly classified under Rate Group 753 for excavation for the period from 1987 to 1992.  The employer claimed that it should be classified under Rate Group 656 for trucking.
The worker appealed a decision closing his vocational rehabilitation file and terminating his temporary disability benefits.

The worker suffered a severe fracture of his ankle when he fell from the roof of a barn in 1966.  He was awarded a 12% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a reassessment of the pension and denying a s. 147(4) supplement.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (supplements, transitional provisions) (wage loss); Discrimination (age); Human rights (mandatory retirement); Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation) (retirement); Supplements, transitional provisions (permanent) (retirement)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying him entitlement to supplementary benefits under s. 147(2) of the Act, subsequent to July 1993.  The worker was injured in 1987 when he was aged 59.   He had been provided with vocational rehabilitation services since 1989.  Decision No. 40/92 had granted this worker entitlement to continuing s. 147(2) benefits and vocational rehabilitation services.  That decision found that the main obstacles to the worker reaching his vocational rehabilitation objective were his disability, his age and the economic climate, but that none of these made the the objective unrealistic or impractical.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back disability which the worker claimed was related either to a foot accident suffered in 1985 or a back injury suffered during a work placement in 1989.

The worker suffered a non-compensable back injury at home in 1983 while moving a heavy plant.  She suffered compensable back injuries at work in 1987 and 1989 while moving patients in a hospital.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting further benefits in 1991.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding the level of the worker's pension for thoracic and shoulder disability.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue a final decision from the Board on entitlement for a number of other accidents.  [4 pages]

The worker suffered a wrist injury in January 1990.  One week later, she suffered further injury in a non-compensable altercation.  The Board originally granted benefits for one week only but later granted further entitlement.  The employer appealed.

The hearing of the employer's appeal was adjourned in the absence of the worker and her representative.  Due to misunderstanding, the worker did not obtain a representative until one week before the hearing.  Another person from the office of the representative asked for an adjournment to allow the representative time to prepare.  The Panel was concerned that it did not have a direct request from the worker or her actual representative but granted the adjournment since the worker's presence was required to make a determination on the real merits and justice of the case.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Injuring process; Chronic pain; Disablement (change in work); Investigation by Tribunal (whether required); Medical opinion (repetitive strain injury); Postal workers (letter sorter); Significant contribution (of employment to disability) (subjective reaction of worker); Stress, mental
DecSummary: The worker worked for the employer for about 12 years primarily as a mail sorter.  In September 1991, she was assigned to an S/L sortation job on a full-shift basis.  She developed left arm, shoulder and neck pain in November 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement.

The worker injured his back when he fell backwards on to a cement floor in June 1991.  He was already receiving a 10% pension for a previous back injury.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting full benefits from February 1992 to September 1992, but granting only 50% benefits from September 1992 until he was reassessed for a pension in January 1994, and denying entitlement for psychotraumatic disability and chronic pain.
The appeal was adjourned pending the receipt of all the worker's claim files.  [5 pages]

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (distinct departure test); Procedure (absent parties); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The issue was whether the plaintiff and defendant drivers were in the course of employment at the time of a motor vehicle accident.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a heart attack.  The worker and his foreman had a history of tension.  On the day in question, the worker and the foreman had an argument, and the foreman told the worker that he was fired.  A meeting was arranged with union and company representatives in which another heated verbal altercation occurred between the worker and the foreman.  The matter was resolved and the worker returned to work.  Soon after, the worker began to experience chest pain.

DecKeywords: Disablement (repetitive work); Osteoarthritis (knee); Tear (meniscus); Transportation industry (truck driver)
DecSummary: The worker was born in 1925.  He retired in January 1989.  In March 1989 the worker rose from a chair and experienced pain and swelling in his right knee.  The worker underwent arthroscopic surgery in June 1989 to repair a degenerative tear of the medial meniscus of his right knee.  The worker argued that he suffered a disablement from his 20 years as a truck driver.  He claimed that emerging from his step van numerous times daily to make his mail pickups resulted in the development of osteoarthritis and the degenerative tear of his medial meniscus.
The worker worked on the production line for a cookie manufacturer for 23 years.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back strain.
The worker suffered a low back strain in 1966 when he sharply twisted his back.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits which the worker claimed in 1989.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer finding that work as a general labourer offered by the employer to the worker was not suitable for the worker, considering his ankle disability.  The Panel found that the work required a lot of standing, as well as climbing ladders and walking on uneven floors.  The Panel concluded that the work was not suitable.

A mail registration clerk appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a shoulder condition, diagnosed as adhesive capsulitis.  The preponderance of medical evidence did not support a relationship between the worker's work and her shoulder condition.
The worker was appealing a decision finding that he was not a worker within the meaning of the Act.  The employer did not appear at the hearing.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a right wrist disability, diagnosed as a  scaffoid fracture.  The worker claimed that he suffered the injury when he was carrying a box into an elevator and the elevator door closed on his wrist.

The worker suffered an inguinal hernia while pushing a heavy cart in April 1987.  He was awarded a pension for permanent disability and for chronic pain.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary total disability benefits subsequent to October 1989.

The worker suffered an ankle injury in 1962 for which he was awarded a 2% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a right hip condition, diagnosed as osteoarthritis from avascular necrosis, which the worker claimed was related to the compensable accident.

The worker appealed a November 1993 decision of the Reinstatement Officer.  The worker injured his low back and right knee in June 1990.  Vocational rehabilitation services were initiated in December 1991.  The worker did not attend physical assessment and reconditioning scheduled for March 1992, claiming that he could not participate because of increased pain which caused a temporary total disability.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (job sharing); Earnings basis (unemployment insurance benefits); Supplements, FEL (Board-authorized program)
DecSummary: The worker was an ambulance attendant who worked on a job-sharing basis (five people for two jobs).  He was injured in April 1990.  He returned to modified work in June 1991 and was laid off in March 1992.  In Decision No. 476/94I, the Panel found that the worker was entitled to a 1% FEL sustainability award in June 1991.  In this decision, the Panel considered the worker's entitlement to a supplement under s. 43(9) from June 1991 to June 1993, and the earnings basis for calculation of benefits.
The worker was struck by a tree in 1941.  He was awarded a pension for low back and left foot disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a pension of 35%.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue entitlement at the Board on a number of related issues resulting from the accident.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Delay (onset of symptoms)
DecSummary: The worker suffered groin pain while lifting at work in November 1989.  He did not lose any time until March 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits in March 1990.

The employer applied for an order requiring the worker to attend a medical examination by a doctor selected by the employer.  The worker was diagnosed as suffering from right elbow tendonitis in January 1993.  The employer offered modified work in December 1993, but it was found to be unsuitable.  The employer wanted the examination to determine the worker's condition, prognosis for recovery, residual restrictions, ability to return to work and any devices and practices necessary to assure comfort while maximizing performance.

DecKeywords: Overpayment; Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation); Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation)
DecSummary: An automotive assembly line worker suffered right shoulder tendonitis in September 1988.  He was awarded a 5% pension in July 1990, but as a result of an error by the Board, he continued to receive full temporary benefits.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting s. 147(4) benefits from October 1990 to October 1992.  The worker appealed denial of s. 147(2) after October 1990 and the recovery of the overpayment.

The worker appealed a decision rating her pension at 0% under the chronic pain disability guidelines.  The Board's assessors appeared to conclude that the worker's complaints were not genuine, but they did not provide any reasons for this conclusion.  The reports of the worker's treating specialists indicated a genuine non-organic disability.  The Panel sent the worker's case back to the Board to review it for a chronic pain disability  and to provide the Panel with reasons for its conclusions.  [5 pages]

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The issue was whether the plaintiff was in the course of employment at the time of a motor vehicle accident.  The defendants were the plaintiff's employer, a co-worker who was the driver of the van in which the plaintiff was a passenger and the lessor of the van.

The worker, who had worked as an assembler for 13 years, suffered a back injury in 1983, for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary supplementary benefits from May 1988 to March 1989 and denying reimbursement for tuition fees and textbooks while he attended university from September 1988 to April 1989.

The worker appealed a decision denying her benefits for chronic pain disability.  She injured her back while lifting at work in 1979, but lost no time from work.  The worker stopped working in June 1981 with a wrist disability.  The Board found she had tendonitis which resulted from the repetitive nature of her job.  This accentuated a pre-existing wrist condition (an old injury, early degenerative changes and a congenital condition).  The worker was discharged from HRC in December 1981 as being fit to return to modified work, with restrictions on use of the right wrist for a three month period.  Three weeks later, the worker fell down some stairs at her home.  She sustained serious comminuted fractures of the right wrist and elbow.

The worker was struck by a falling tree in 1967.  He returned to work two weeks later.  He was awarded a 30% pension for low back disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for shoulder and neck problems in 1986.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (supplements, temporary) (extension); Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation); Supplements, temporary; Supplements, transitional provisions
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in 1984, for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting supplements subsequent to a lay-off in January 1989, and classification of a lay-off in 1992 as an aggravation of the compensable injury rather than as a new accident.

The worker was appealing denial of temporary benefits beyond a certain date.  The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue a final decision from the Board regarding FEL entitlement.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Carpal tunnel syndrome; Disablement (nature of work)
DecSummary: A health care aide suffered shoulder, neck and low back strain while lifting a patient in January 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (benefit to the employer); In the course of employment (personal activity); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Right to sue
DecSummary: The issue in this s. 17 application was whether the parties to a court action were in the course of their employment at the time of the motor vehicle collision in which they were involved.
The worker had a compensable heart attack in 1984.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a 50% pension for the worker's residual cardiac condition.

DecKeywords: Supplements, temporary; Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation)
DecSummary: The worker injured his back at work in December 1983.  He returned to his regular job as a hospital porter in June 1984.  The worker was fired in September 1984 when he refused to do a particular job.  The employer claimed that the worker refused because he said that he had too much work already.  The worker worker claimed that he refused because his back was hurting.  The worker did not work after September 1984.  The worker was awarded a 10% pension in May 1987.  The worker received a s. 147(4) supplement from July 1989 to February 1992.

The worker suffered a right elbow injury in August 1988.  In October 1989, she was awarded a 3% pension for organic disability.  In October 1991, this was replaced by a 10% pension for chronic pain.  The worker appealed the level of her pension and denial of a s. 147(4) supplement subsequent to October 1991.

The worker appealed a decision denying his claim for work-related stress.  On July 2, 1991 he had a confrontation with his supervisor.  He took time off work and filed a claim for sickness and accident benefits under the company's disability insurance scheme.  The worker had previously requested a transfer to another department.  On July 8, 1991 the worker's family doctor diagnosed the worker as having reactive anxiety state and recommended that he change jobs.

DecKeywords: Overpayment; Presumptions (termination of re-employment); Re-employment (duration of obligation); Re-employment (termination) (financial viability)
DecSummary: The worker was injured in April 1991.  He returned to modified work in October 1991, and to regular work later that month.  In September 1992, just more than six months after his return to work, the worker's employment was terminated.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer breached its re-employment obligations.
The hearing was adjourned due to the absence of the worker.  The worker was involved in a motor vehicle accident while on his way to the hearing.
The hearing was adjourned and Tribunal counsel was directed to obtain further medical evidence.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a number of injuries when he fell four feet in June 1987.  He was able to return to work, but stopped working again in March 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits after March 1988.

The worker suffered a back injury in 1988 for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  He laid off due to a recurrence in October 1990.  Prior to that lay-off, he enrolled in a community college program in stationary engineering.  He completed requirements for certification as a fourth class stationary engineer but was unable to complete the requirements for a third class stationary engineer.  The Board helped the worker with a job search and arranged a 16-week work placement but the worker was unable to obtain permanent employment.  The Board terminated VR services and supplementary benefits at the end of September 1992.  The worker appealed.
The employer's application to reconsider Decision No. 194/94L was denied.  [4 pages]

The worker suffered a burn injury to his hand in January 1984.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for carpal tunnel syndrome diagnosed in 1988 or a stroke diagnosed in 1991.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a hand injury in September 1980.  The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying temporary benefits subsequent to February 1982.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 352/94 was denied.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Adjournment (additional medical evidence); Three week rule (documents)
DecSummary: The worker delivered two new books of evidence to the Tribunal on the three week rule deadline and to the employer past the deadline.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue entitlement at the Board for another condition.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a back injury in December 1990.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the worker was entitled to temporary benefits subsequent to December 1991.  On the evidence, work to which the worker returned in October 1991 was not suitable.  Bending and lifting required for the job aggravated the worker's condition.
The appeal was withdrawn.  There was no final decision of the Board on the only issue in dispute.  [3 pages]

The worker was appealing a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer did not breach its re-employment obligations.  Since filing this appeal, a Hearings Officer confirmed initial entitlement.  The employer was appealing that decision, claiming that the worker was intoxicated, and that the accident was attributable solely to the serious and wilful misconduct of the worker.

The worker was appealing a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer did not breach its re-employment obligations.  The worker requested that the Tribunal order and pay for the transcript of the Reinstatement Officer hearing.

The worker suffered a whiplash injury in a compensable motor vehicle accident in May 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement when the worker stopped working in October 1991.

DecKeywords: Carpal tunnel syndrome; Disablement (repetitive work); Investigation by Tribunal; Medical report (opinion of medical assessor)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision granting the worker benefits for bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome.  The worker was aged 50 and had been working as a warehouse stock clerk for five years at the time of the onset of symptoms.

The worker suffered a dislocated shoulder in a compensable accident in 1981 when he was thrown in the air and fell to the ground.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for neck disability and headaches.

The worker suffered a low back strain in August 1990 when she sneezed as she was lifting an object.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting only 50% benefits from November 1990 to July 1989.
The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer breached its re-employment obligations and imposing a penalty of about $16,000.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (manufacturing) (meat and fish products); Discretion, Board (class of employer); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (over Board process)
DecSummary: The employer was a meat processor.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying reclassification of the employer from Rate Group 207 for manufacturing of meat and fish products to a different rate group with a lower risk of accident.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (manufacturing) (meat and fish products); Discretion, Board (class of employer); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (over Board process)
DecSummary: The employer's appeal from a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding classification in Rate Group 207 for manufacturing of meat and fish products was dismissed for the reasons in Decision No. 888/94.  [2 pages]

A health care aide suffered a wrist injury on August 5, 1992, while restraining a patient.  She did not lose time or seek medical treatment.  She began to experience further wrist problems at home on August 24, while cleaning a storm window.  She saw her doctor on August 26.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement subsequent to August 26.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (manufacturing) (meat and fish products); Discretion, Board (class of employer); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (over Board process)
DecSummary: The employer's appeal from a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding classification in Rate Group 207 for manufacturing of meat and fish products was dismissed for the reasons in Decision No. 888/94.  [2 pages]
The hearing was adjourned to obtain additional evidence.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Class of employer (manufacturing) (meat and fish products); Discretion, Board (class of employer); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (over Board process)
DecSummary: The employer's appeal from a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding classification in Rate Group 207 for manufacturing of meat and fish products was dismissed for the reasons in Decision No. 888/94.  [2 pages]

The worker suffered a back injury in 1979 for which she was awarded a 10% pension.  The worker also suffered back and shoulder injuries in another accident in 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain.

The hearing was adjourned so that Tribunal counsel could assess the relevance of a large number of documents which, through misunderstanding, had not been forwarded to the Tribunal or the employer.  [3 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a low back injury which the worker claimed he suffered at work on July 31, 1992.  After a three-day weekend, the worker returned to work for four days.  On August 7, 1992, his employment was terminated.
The worker suffered a wrist injury in November 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer denying supplementary benefits under s. 43(9) in July 1993 and after November 1993.
The appeal was withdrawn due to the illness of the worker.  [3 pages]

The worker was exposed to glue fumes at work over a six-month period in 1988.  The worker began to experience migraine headaches in March 1988, and stopped working in June 1988.  The Board granted entitlement until December 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement.

DecKeywords: Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation); Temporary disability (beyond pension level)
DecSummary: The worker suffered an electric shock in July 1982.  He was awarded a 5% pension for organic disability and a 10% pension for non-organic disability.  The worker received supplementary benefits until September 1, 1989.  On September 12, 1989, he found a job but aggravated his condition on September 24.  Temporary benefits were discontinued on December 13.  The worker appealed denial of further temporary and supplementary benefits.

After the hearing of the worker's appeal in Sudbury, the Panel decided to obtain additional medical evidence.  The worker's representative refused to make only written submissions concerning the additional evidence.  He wanted to make his submissions face-to-face.  It was agreed to set up a video conference.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying transfer of part of the costs of the worker's claim to the Administrative Fund.  The worker was injured in a fall in August 1990.  The employer submitted that by November 1990, the worker was capable of returning to work but that the Board sought a second medical opinion which delayed implementation of vocational rehabilitation services until April 1991.  At that point the Board recommended a referral to the Regional Evaluation Centre but this was not done.  By the time the worker was evaluated in October 1991, he had developed chronic pain.  This resulted in greatly increased costs to the employer.  The employer claimed that this was caused by the Board's intervention in the worker's medical treatment.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (earnings basis) (learner); Earnings basis (learner); Earnings basis (nominal remuneration)
DecSummary: In 1984, the worker was a full-time student at a community college in a millwright apprenticeship course.  She was assigned to work part-time for an employer and suffered an arm injury, for which she received a pension. The worker appealed a Hearings Officer decision as to the earnings basis for calculation of benefits.
The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting initial entitlement for a left shoulder condition disablement from repetitive work wrapping small items.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (witness availability); Delay (onset of symptoms); Rehabilitation (cooperation) (relinquishing employment on own volition)
DecSummary: The worker fell at work on July 23, 1987, while carrying a tub weighing about 25 pounds.  She fell on her back, striking her elbow as she fell, with the tub landing on her foot.  The Board accepted entitlement for the foot injury.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for neck, shoulder, chest and back injuries which the worker claimed she also suffered in the accident and denying temporary benefits after August 28, 1987.

The worker suffered an upper back and shoulder injury in February 1990.  She stopped work again in August 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits from August 1990 to June 1991.

The worker suffered a prolapsed disc in August 1983, for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a recurrence while changing a tire on his car.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Pensions (assessment) (chronic pain); Supplements, temporary; Supplements, transitional provisions
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back strain in a lifting incident in May 1988.  She was discharged from HRC to return to work in February 1989.  She left work after a few hours.  The Board terminated benefits in February 1989 but later decided to pay benefits until May 1989 due to lack of proper notification of the termination.  She was awarded a 15% pension in June 1989.  The worker found part-time employment as a cleaner at the church which she attended.  She stopped working in January 1992, claiming a recurrence.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement to temporary benefits subsequent to May 1989, denying entitlement for chronic pain, denying entitlement for the recurrence in January 1992 and denying a pension supplement.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (manufacturing) (meat and fish products); Discretion, Board (class of employer); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (over Board process)
DecSummary: The employer's appeal from a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding classification in Rate Group 207 for manufacturing of meat and fish products was dismissed for the reasons in Decision No. 888/94.  [2 pages]
A construction worker suffered injuries to multiple parts of his body when he fell 11 feet in April 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits.

DecKeywords: Overpayment; Supplements, transitional provisions (calculation) (Canada Pension Plan)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury for which he was awarded a 20% pension.  In February 1992, he began receiving a disability pension under the Canada Pension Plan.  In August 1992, the worker began receiving a pension supplement under s. 147(2).  In January 1993, the Board began reducing the worker's supplement under s. 147(11) due to receipt of benefits under the Canada Pension Plan.  The worker appealed a decision of the Board to recover the overpayment for the period from August 1992 to January 1993.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue a final decision at the Board on related issues.  [3 pages]

The worker laid off work due to a back sprain in the first week of  November 1992.  He had begun working with the accident employer in late September 1992 as a concrete worker in the construction industry.  The worker initially did skreeting of concrete floors.  However, during the last few weeks before his lay-off, he had been operating a vibrator during the pouring of concrete walls.  On the weekend before his lay-off, the worker rented a jackhammer to break concrete so that a drain could be relocated in the basement of his home.
The request to reconsider Decision No. 246/94 was dismissed.  There was no new evidence or error of law.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (disc, degeneration); Chronic pain; Disc, herniated; Medical opinion (disc, herniated); Subsequent incidents (outside work)
DecSummary: In June 1990 the worker stopped working due to back pain.  She was awarded benefits for aggravation of a pre-existing condition.  The worker returned to work in November 1990.  In the last week of June 1991, the worker's job was changed to one with heavier duties.  The worker communicated her concerns about worsening pain to her supervisor.  While at home on June 30, 1991, the worker experienced a sudden onset of back pain and she sought immediate medical attention.  A herniated disc was diagnosed and surgery was performed.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (personal activity); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work); In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue
DecSummary: The worker was involved in a fatal motor vehicle accident.  He had completed an out-of-town delivery, but it was not known where he was going when the accident occurred.  Assuming that the worker was travelling from the last delivery site, the worker was travelling on a route away from his home, but towards his office, at the time of the accident. The accident site was relatively close to the office. Though the office was closed at the time of the accident, the worker had a key.

The worker was injured in January 1986.  In January 1990, the Hearings Officer ordered that the worker be assessed for a pension and directed that, if a pension were awarded, the pension would be retroactive to October 1986.  In November 1990, the worker was awarded a 10% pension retroactive to October 1986.

A 47-year-old worker at a correctional institution suffered a heart attack in January 1990.  The worker related the heart attack to the stressful nature of his job and to a specific incident in April 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the heart attack.
The hearing of the employer's appeal was adjourned to wait for a final decision from the Board on a related issue.  [4 pages]

The worker was a machine operator.  He usually operated a drilling machine but sometimes operated a milling machine.  The worker claimed he suffered a low back pain while working one day on the milling machine.  He had to feed hinges into the milling machine.  He claimed the back pain was caused by raking the hinges out of a bin in order to take them to the machine.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement.

The worker suffered a non-compensable low back injury which resulted in a two-level spinal fusion with a bone graft in February 1985.  He did reasonably heavy work as an apprentice for a tool and die company in 1986 and 1987.  The worker began delivering parcels for the accident employer in August 1987.  He continued this job until April 1991, when he laid off work because of back pain.  The worker claimed that his lay-off was related to an aggravation of a previously asymptomatic back condition caused by his general job duties as a delivery person, especially bending, twisting and lifting.

DecKeywords: Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation); Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary) (retirement)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable injury in June 1984.  In 1986, he was awarded a 5% pension for shoulder disability.  The worker returned to modified work as a tram driver.  When this work was no longer available, the worker was given cleaning duties.  He had recurrences in December 1986 and October 1987.  In February 1988, the worker accepted a company disability plan for early retirement.  The Board considered this a voluntary removal from the workforce.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying supplementary benefits subsequent to February 1988.

DecKeywords: Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (preexisting condition)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury when lifting in July 1991.  In November 1992, she underwent surgery for a herniated disc.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying SIEF relief.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Freedom of Information (confidentiality provision)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  The Panel agreed with Decision No. 169/94 that the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act did not prevent the Tribunal from releasing this information.  [5 pages]

The worker suffered knee injuries in 1985 and 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a back condition which the worker claimed was related to the compensable accidents.

The worker applied for an order that he was not required to attend a medical examination requested by the employer.  The employer had valid compensation goals regarding entitlement to benefits and appropriateness of modified work.

DecKeywords: Supplements, temporary; Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary) (participation in rehabilitation)
DecSummary: The worker suffered injuries in 1971 and 1978 for which he was awarded a 25% pension.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting supplementary benefits retroactively for the period from June 1988 to July 1992.

The worker suffered a non-compensable back injury in 1977.  He suffered compensable back injuries in 1986, 1987 and 1989.  In 1990, the worker injured his back again as he got out of his car.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits in 1990.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (non-medical information) (psychologist's report); Medical examination (employer request) (medical practitioner); Procedure (Board) (access to worker file); Words and phrases (medical examination); Words and phrases (medical practitioner); Words and phrases (medical reports)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Board to release to the employer a report by a psychologist.  Section 71(5) provides that, prior to granting access to an employer,  the Board must give workers an opportunity to object to release of medical reports and opinions.  The issue was whether the report of the psychologist was a medical report within the meaning of s. 71.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (operation of restaurant business); Schedule 1 employer (for profit or gain)
DecSummary: The worker was a waiter at a cafe operated by a social club.  The Hearings Officer found that the employer was a mixed industry - part restaurant business which was compulsorily covered by the Act, and part social club which was not covered by the Act.  The Hearings Officer concluded that s. 7 of Reg. 1102 applied so that the employer was dealt with as if all the operations were under Schedule 1.  The employer appealed, claiming that it was not an industry within Schedule 1.

The worker slipped and fell off a bulldozer in 1977.  He was awarded benefits for shoulder and cervical disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back disability.

DecKeywords: Significant contribution (of compensable accident to disability)
DecSummary: The worker's jaw was fractured in October 1988 when he was struck by a lever.  He underwent immediate reconstructive surgery.  He underwent further reconstructive surgery in March 1989.  He underwent surgery again in July 1989 due to nerve compression.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the surgery in July 1989.

A nurse injured her back while supporting a patient in November 1990.  In January 1991, she slipped and fell, and was awarded benefits for neck, hip and leg injuries.  In May 1991, a herniated disc was diagnosed.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits in May 1991.

The worker was awarded benefits from July 1990 to November 1990, for right wrist and arm disability which aggravated preexisting Paget's disease and osteoporosis.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying continuing entitlement after November 1990.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Procedure (absent parties) (access to worker file)
DecSummary: The Panel proceeded, in the absence of the worker, with the hearing of the worker's appeal from a decision to grant access to his file to the employer.

The worker requested reconsideration of Decision No. 605/94 in which the Panel increased the worker's pension from 2% to 10% retroactive to February 1991. The worker submitted that the 2% pension was retroactive to the date of the accident and  that the increase should also be retroactive to the date of the accident.
After consulting with his representative, the worker withdrew his appeal of a decision granting access to his file to the employer.  [3 pages]

The worker fell from a bulldozer in November 1990.  He continued to work until a general lay-off in February 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits in February 1991.
The worker suffered a low back strain in September 1985 and returned to work in December 1985.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement in August 1991.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Disc, herniated
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back strain in August 1985 when he turned and pulled a heavy object.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement in 1990.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic obstructive lung disease.  The Panel accepted a thorough report from the worker's treating respirologist that the worker was suffering from an early form of chronic obstructive lung disease (chronic bronchitis with an asthmatic component) which was related to exposure at work to irritants and inhalants.

The worker was appealing a finding that she refused suitable work.  The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to return to the Board for a final decision on the issue of whether the worker was partially or totally disabled.  [4 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for psoriatic arthritis, which the worker related to falls at work in 1967 and 1973.  The worker did not claim entitlement until 1987.
The worker suffered four low back strains between 1983 and 1985.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a pension for permanent disability.

The worker suffered a dislocated shoulder in June 1989.  He dislocated the shoulder again in a non-compensable motor vehicle accident in February 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further entitlement in February 1990.

The worker was not entitled to supplementary benefits under s. 147(2) during a lay-off of two months.  The Panel was satisfied that the lay-off was not related to the worker's compensable disability, but rather was due to employment circumstances.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Personal coverage (actual earnings); Personal coverage (estimated earnings); Reconsideration (error of law); Right to sue
DecSummary: The plaintiff in a civil case applied to reconsider Decision No. 211/94 in which the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  Decision No. 211/94 focused on whether the plaintiff was in the course of employment.  It was admitted at the original hearing that she was a deemed worker because she had personal coverage.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Rehabilitation, vocational (program not offered by Board); Rehabilitation, vocational (suitability of program) (program chosen by worker); Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary)
DecSummary: The worker strained his shoulder in November 1988 and was paid temporary benefits.  In July 1990 he returned to lower paying modified work and his vocational rehabilitation file was closed.  His s. 147(2) benefits were terminated and he instead received wage loss differential payments under s. 147(4).  The modified work was frequently changed, but always involved repetitive sustained use of  the worker's arm, contrary to his restrictions, and often involved heavy lifting and above shoulder work, contrary to his restrictions.  In November 1990 the worker was laid off by his employer due to a work shortage.  The only work available was a general labouring job that required very heavy lifting.  The Board did not restore the worker's  s. 147(2)  benefits until December 1992.

The worker, a car mechanic, suffered a neck and shoulder injury in March 1986 when the hood of a van fell on him.  He returned to work the next day.  He laid off in January 1988 because of pain.  In October 1988, he was diagnosed with spinal stenosis at C3-4.  He underwent a laminectomy and left foramenotomy.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer which denied benefits from January 1988 to October 1988 on the basis that the worker was not totally disabled but granted benefits from the time of the surgery in October 1988.

A steam fitter/pipe fitter appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for bilateral osteoarthritis of the knees which the worker related to the nature of his work which involved heavy lifting, climbing, kneeling and working on slopes.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Disablement (repetitive work); Farming; Osteoarthritis (hip); Osteoarthritis (knee)
DecSummary: A farmer suffered a low back injury in 1966 when he was lifting a heavy object.  He suffered a further low back injury in 1987 as he tried to loosen a nut with a wrench.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for osteoarthritis of the hips and knees which the worker related to the compensable accidents or to the nature of his work as a farmer.
The worker suffered a back injury in 1987.  In 1989, he was awarded a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying payment of the pension as a lump sum.

DecKeywords: Apportionment (negligence); Supplier of motor vehicle, machinery or equipment
DecSummary: The worker was injured when a chair on which she was sitting collapsed.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying transfer of the costs of the accident to the manufacturer and supplier of the chair.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (employer's premises); In the course of employment (reasonably incidental activity test); Right to sue; Worker (contract of service) (commencement); Worker (contract of service) (employment relationship)
DecSummary: The defendant in a civil case brought an application under s. 17.  The issues were whether the plaintiff was a worker and, if so, whether she was in the course of employment at the time of the accident.

The worker suffered a wrist injury in an accident in 1977.  He also suffered carpal tunnel syndrome from the nature of his work in 1987.  He underwent surgery in 1987.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a pension for wrist disability.

The worker was exposed to chemicals at work for four days in July 1985 that were known to cause dermatitis.  The worker received benefits until December 1985.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying ongoing entitlement.
The hearing was adjourned and would be reconvened for two additional days of hearing due to the complexities of the evidence and the need to hear evidence from a Tribunal assessor.  [5 pages]

A seamstress suffered a back injury in 1983.  In 1990, she was awarded a one-year provisional 15% pension for chronic pain.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits for chronic pain after the one-year period and denying s. 147(4) supplementary benefits.

DecKeywords: Presumptions (termination of re-employment); Re-employment (collective agreement) (seniority provisions) (recall rights); Re-employment (obligation to re-employ); Re-employment (termination)
DecSummary: The worker was a temporary employee who had been working for the employer for 18 months.  In October 1990, he was given notice of termination effective November 30, 1990.  He was injured on November 6, and was fit to return to work on November 19.  His employment was terminated on November 30 as scheduled.  The collective agreement provided a right to be rehired for six months.  In May 1991 (within the six months), the employer requisitioned two temporary employees.  In June 1991 (after the six months), the employees were hired.  The worker was not rehired.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that it breached its re-employment obligations.

The worker requested reconsideration of Decision No. 606/94 which denied the worker a continuing wage loss supplement.  The worker's arguments on the reconsideration had been fully considered in the original decision.  The reconsideration request was denied.  [5 pages]

The worker began to experience difficulties with his neck, upper back and shoulder in November 1991 which he reported to his doctor in December 1991.  The worker related this to his employment as a cement finisher which involved heavy concrete raking work and repetitive cement grinding work.  The worker was off work for about a year, prior to September 1991, due to a lack of work.  During this period, he constructed a new home for his family and his wife's home-based business.  The worker was under considerable stress from November 1991 to January 1992.  There were significant financial concerns, as well as family and emotional conflicts.  The worker also looked after his wife and children during her convalescence from injuries received in a motor vehicle accident.  The worker was, and still is, emotionally fragile.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 33/94 was denied.  The worker did not submit any new arguments.  New medical reports did not relate the worker's condition to the compensable accident.  [5 pages]
The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 184/94 was denied.  [3 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a neck and shoulder injury which the worker claimed he suffered as a result of carrying heavy planks on his shoulder in October 1988.  The worker did not claim entitlement until January 1990.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (commutation) (restored benefits); Commutation (calculation) (discount rate); Commutation (restored benefits) (deductions) (escalation); Interest
DecSummary: The worker suffered below-knee amputation of both legs in an accident in 1942.  He was awarded an 80% pension.  In 1987, the pension was increased to 100% retroactive to 1948.  In Decision No. 153/94LM, the Panel granted full arrears of the increase.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (job search); Worker (long term service)
DecSummary: The worker, a mail service courier, slipped and fell in December 1987.  She injured her hip and her lower back.  She received temporary total benefits until March 1988 and again from November 1988 to March 1989.  The worker sought benefits from March 1989 to December 1990.

DecKeywords: Apportionment (industrial disease) (hearing loss); Apportionment (Schedule 1 and 2 employers); Hearing loss
DecSummary: The worker worked for various employers in the construction industry from 1955 to 1976.  From 1976 to 1986, he worked for a board of education, a Schedule 2 employer, mostly in its carpentry shop.  The Board granted the worker a pension for hearing loss, which it found resulted both from his work in construction and for the Schedule 2 employer.  The Board charged the full cost of the claim to the Schedule 2 employer pursuant to s. 134(2).  The employer appealed.

The worker suffered shoulder, chest and knee injuries in a fall at work in March 1990.  The worker returned to work for a work trial in May 1991 but did not complete the program.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits after June 1991.

The worker suffered a shoulder and upper back injury in March 1988 when he slipped while carrying a heavy box.  He returned to work in March 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a permanent disability award.

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation); Rehabilitation, vocational (suitability of program)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back strain in August 1990.  He was awarded a 35% NEL award for chronic pain.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer denying further rehabilitation services and supplementary benefits after June 1992.

The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer breached its re-employment obligations, assessing a penalty and awarding benefits to the worker.  The worker suffered a back injury in June 1992 and returned to work in November 1992.  There was a hostile discussion between the worker and his supervisor.  In December 1992, there was a further incident between the worker and his supervisor.  There were allegations of assault by both.  The police were called and there were criminal proceedings.  The worker's employment was terminated a few days later.

The worker suffered a low back injury in 1978 for which he was awarded a 35% pension.  He suffered an aggravation in 1990 while working for a different employer.  The Board set up a new claim number for the occurrence in 1990.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying continuing temporary benefits from June 1991 to March 1992 for disability resulting from the 1990 accident.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a left arm disability which the worker claimed he suffered in an accident at work in 1988 when he was closing the tailgate of his truck.  The accident was unwitnessed and there were some discrepancies in the evidence.  However, the Panel found the worker credible.  Further, there was supportive evidence from the worker's foreman that the worker reported an injury and ongoing complaints.

The worker suffered a thoracic spine strain in May 1986.  She returned to modified work in March 1988.  She received further benefits for an aggravation in June, July and August 1988.  She received benefits from November 1988 to October 1989 for fibrositis.  In May 1988, she was awarded a 10% provisional pension for fibrositis.  This was confirmed and made permanent under the chronic pain guidelines in October 1989.  The worker appealed denial of an increase in the pension and denial of temporary benefits from October 1989 until her return to work in June 1990, as well as a number of days in November 1990 and March 1991, and subsequent to April 1991.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Continuing entitlement
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying her temporary benefits after November 1991.  The worker performed repetitive work as a press operator when she began to receive treatment for tendonitis in her arms in 1990.  There was continuity of complaint from August 1990 until at least July 1995.  The same restrictions for her return to full-time modified work were in place from August 1991 to February 1995.  The worker was receiving injections for her shoulder and attended physiotherapy.  The worker returned to full-time work in 1995 though she still had pain in her shoulder.

The employer appealed continuing entitlement regarding an accident in 1992.  In Decision No. 82/94I, the hearing was adjourned to wait for a final decision of the Board regarding an earlier accident in 1990.  The Board confirmed compensability of the 1990 accident.  After reviewing the matter, the employer asked to withdraw the appeal.  The worker requested that the Panel impose conditions on the employer's right to re-file the appeal.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome which the worker claimed was related to the repetitive nature of her work on an automobile assembly line from 1983 to 1986.

The worker suffered a left knee injury in 1984 for which she was awarded a 12% pension.  In 1986, she developed right knee problems.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for right knee disability as a sequela of the left knee disability.

The employer appealed a decision granting the worker initial entitlement for a bilateral wrist condition diagnosed as De Quervain's disease.  The worker started her job as a purchasing clerk in August 1988.  For each order, she had to separate a six-copy purchase order.  The worker processed an average of 50 orders daily, but with peaks of up to 150 orders per day.  She did extensive keyboard data entry without the benefit of ergonomic equipment which would have provided rest for her wrists.  The onset of symptoms required the worker to do light duty work for a few weeks each time in September 1989, February 1990 and June 1990.  In June 1990, when it was clear that long-term light duty work was not available, the worker quit her employment.

The worker had a back disability for which he was receiving a 20% pension.  He suffered a recurrence in June 1982.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting temporary benefits to September 1992 but denying temporary benefits from then until November 1992.
The appeal was withdrawn at the request of the worker's representative.  The worker was apparently working in the United States and the representative was unable to locate him.  [3 pages]
